sources.title: Japanese yen nears 160 per dollar as US rate hike bets strengthen
sources.text:
Japanese yen nears 160 per dollar as US rate hike bets strengthen
The Japanese yen fell to its weakest level in more than two months against the US dollar on Thursday, moving close to the psychologically important 160-per-dollar mark as expectations of further US interest rate hikes widened the policy gap between Washington and Tokyo.
The dollar rose as high as 159.94 yen, its strongest level against the Japanese currency in more than two months, according to Reuters.
The yen’s renewed weakness prompted fresh warnings from Japanese authorities over the possibility of intervention in the foreign exchange market.
Japan’s top currency diplomat Atsushi Mimura said recent currency movements had been excessively rapid and warned traders not to forget Tokyo’s yen-buying interventions earlier this year.
“It’s still too early to forget what happened this summer,” Mimura said, referring to intervention carried out in late July and early August, including one operation conducted jointly with the United States.
Strong US inflation boosts dollar
The dollar has strengthened broadly after hotter-than-expected US inflation data increased expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates again.
US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, above forecasts for a 0.3% increase, while core inflation also came in stronger than expected. The data prompted investors to consider the possibility of a larger 50-basis-point rate hike at the Federal Reserve’s December meeting.
Hawkish comments from Federal Reserve officials have added to those expectations, supporting US Treasury yields and the dollar.
Weak yen raises pressure on Japan
The yen’s depreciation is becoming increasingly problematic for Japan because it raises the cost of imported energy, food and raw materials.
Japan’s yen-based import price index rose 24.8% in October from a year earlier, highlighting the inflationary impact of the weaker currency.
At the same time, the Bank of Japan faces its own policy dilemma. Wholesale inflation accelerated to 7.1% in October, strengthening expectations that the central bank could raise its policy rate again at its December 17-18 meeting.
Some analysts expect the Bank of Japan to increase rates from 1.25% to 1.5%, although policymakers remain divided over how quickly monetary policy should be tightened.
Markets are now closely watching the 160-yen level, which could increase pressure on Tokyo to intervene if the currency continues to weaken sharply.

sources.title: Fed December Rate Hike All but Certain as Yen Nears 160 Line, Indonesian Rupiah Hits Record Low
sources.text:
Fed December Rate Hike All but Certain as Yen Nears 160 Line, Indonesian Rupiah Hits Record Low
An unexpectedly strong US inflation reading, combined with a barrage of hawkish signals from Federal Reserve officials, has left the market all but certain of another rate hike in December. Dollar buying has regrouped, and Asian currencies broadly weakened on Thursday (Nov. 12). The yen touched ¥159.90 per dollar intraday, a roughly two-month low and just a step away from the psychological 160 mark, while the Indonesian Rupiah broke through the 18,200 level to set a record low.
According to Nikkei Asia, the yen came under pressure from the start of Tokyo trading hours, hitting a low of 159.90 — its weakest showing since it broke through 160 in early September. As of 3 p.m. Japan time (1 a.m. EST on Nov. 12), the yen traded at ¥159.70 per dollar, down about 0.5% on the day. The US Dollar Index rose in tandem to 103, its highest level since April last year, reflecting broad dollar strength against the yen, the euro and other major currencies.
The trigger for this dollar offensive was US October consumer price index data that came in above market expectations. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% month-over-month, exceeding the 0.2% forecast. The policy-sensitive US 2-year Treasury yield jumped in response, and the 10-year yield also approached the 5% mark, with the rate differential pushing money straight into the dollar.
Comments from Federal Reserve officials added fuel to the fire. Governor Christopher Waller said before the data release that even if October inflation cooled, he would still "support a 25-basis-point increase in the policy rate at the December FOMC meeting." He also set a condition: if core CPI rose 0.3% or more month-over-month, a 50-basis-point hike should be evaluated. The actual figure landed right at 0.3%, and the market immediately amplified its interpretation. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan hinted that stronger inflation could require a faster pace of tightening, while Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee described the price report as "another disturbing, even bordering on troubling, report."
The CME FedWatch tool showed the market sees a 100% probability of a Federal Reserve rate hike at the December meeting, with some investors even beginning to bet on a 50-basis-point move at once. The Fed only began raising rates in September this year — its first hike in more than three years — lifting the overnight benchmark rate by a quarter point to a range of 3.75% to 4.0%.
Note: Yen quotes are as of 3 p.m. Japan time on Nov. 12; yields are intraday quotes.
As the yen approached 160, Japan's top currency official Atsushi Mimura warned market participants that it was "too early" to forget this summer's intervention. He was referring to the joint currency market intervention by Japan and the US in late July to support the yen. The yen rebounded slightly right after Mimura's remarks, showing that verbal intervention still has some deterrent effect.
However, this round of yen weakness differs from the summer situation. The Bank of Japan's latest meeting opinion summary showed that policymakers remain highly vigilant about upside inflation risks and support further rate hikes, with market bets on an additional hike at the December meeting holding above 70%. Driven by the surge in US Treasury yields, Japan's 10-year benchmark government bond yield also climbed to 2.785% on the day. This means Japan and the US are tightening simultaneously, and the yen's selling pressure is not a one-way rout — the battle over the 160 line will be especially fierce.
Lloyd Chan, senior FX analyst for global markets research at Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG), noted that "a strengthening dollar is once again becoming the main headwind for Asian currencies." He believes that a rising Dollar Index, climbing Treasury yields and high oil prices are making the region's near-term macroeconomic environment challenging.
Asian currencies weakened almost across the board. The Philippine peso, Taiwan dollar, Australian Dollar and Indonesian Rupiah all fell against the dollar, with the Australian Dollar hitting its lowest since late January and the Indonesian Rupiah setting a record low after breaking through 18,200. Indonesian political uncertainty deepened the selling pressure: Vice President Gibran Rakabuming formally resigned on Thursday after a controversy over his high school education credentials and allegations of wiretapping President Prabowo Subianto.
Some analysts also believe the market's imagination about a 50-basis-point move is overdone. Seiji Katsurahata, an economist at Dai-ichi Life Research Institute, noted that current market speculation about a 50-basis-point Fed hike in December appears to be an overreaction; as pricing eventually settles on a 25-basis-point hike, short-term Treasury yields should normalize and the dollar's upside is expected to be limited.
Looking back at this year's trajectory, the yen broke through 160 in late August — the first time since the joint Japan-US intervention in late July. At that time, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh hinted at the Jackson Hole central bank symposium in Wyoming that US rates might need to stay high for longer, driving the dollar higher. After that, supported by market speculation that authorities would intervene again and a string of verbal warnings from Japanese officials, the yen roughly stabilized in the 157-158 range. Now that line of defense has been breached.
For investors, the near-term focus is on US employment data and the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index due before the December meeting, which will determine whether bets on a 50-basis-point move continue to build or fade. If the yen formally breaks through 160, whether Japanese authorities shift from verbal warnings to actual market entry will be the most sensitive variable for Asian FX markets. Meanwhile, the Indonesian Rupiah's record low and Indonesia's political turmoil mean that capital outflow pressure on emerging Asian assets will be hard to ease anytime soon.

sources.title: Hot US Inflation Drags the Yen Close to 160. Will Japan Step In Again?
sources.text:
The dollar climbed to 159.94 yen early Thursday in Tokyo, its strongest level in more than two months. Hot US inflation data and rising bets on a Federal Reserve (Fed) rate hike drove the move.
That leaves the yen just short of 160, a level markets watch for signs of Japanese intervention. Japan spent a record sum supporting the yen this year, but most of those gains have since faded.
Why a Hawkish Bank of Japan Isn't Rescuing the Yen
US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October from September, above the 0.23% forecast. The odds of a December 9 Fed rate hike then rose to 100%, CME FedWatch data showed.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller had also said a half-point hike should be considered if October inflation ran hot. Those bets lifted the US dollar index to a 19-month high.
In Japan, wholesale prices rose 7.1% in October from a year earlier, above the 6.5% forecast. Many analysts expect the Bank of Japan (BOJ) to lift rates to 1.5% from 1.25% on December 17–18.
However, a quarter-point BOJ hike would only match a quarter-point Fed move. The gap between US and Japanese rates would stay the same. A half-point Fed hike would widen it further.
With rate moves unlikely to close that gap soon, Japan's Finance Ministry has become the yen's main backstop.
Follow us on X to get the latest news as it happens
Tokyo's Warning Carries a Costly Track Record
The ministry sent a fresh signal on Thursday. Atsushi Mimura, its vice minister for international affairs, spoke to reporters as the yen neared 160.
      "I won't comment on the current exchange-rate level, but I believe recent currency moves have been excessively rapid," he said.
He also said it was still too early to forget what happened this summer. Ministry data show Japan spent ¥15.40 trillion on July 30, July 31 and August 3. That lifted the year's total past ¥27 trillion.
The previous annual record was about ¥15 trillion, set in 2024. The July 30 operation alone reached ¥7.98 trillion, a single-day record.
Within a month, the yen weakened again to 160.16 per dollar. It had given up more than half its gains from the summer operations.
That suggests intervention can buy time but cannot close the rate gap. A weak yen also raises Japan's import bill. Import prices jumped 24.8% in yen terms, according to the latest producer price data.
That adds pressure on the Bank of Japan (BOJ) before its December 17-18 policy meeting.
For Bitcoin (BTC), a sudden yen jump could still force traders to unwind yen-funded carry trades. The first test comes on December 9, when the Fed decides whether that gap widens again.

sources.title: Japanese Yen recovers from two-month low as BoJ rate hike bets meet intervention risk
sources.text:
The USD/JPY pair attracts some sellers during the Asian session on Thursday, snapping a two-day winning streak to its highest level since early September, around the 160.00 psychological mark touched the previous day. Spot prices, however, show some resilience below mid-159.00s, warranting some caution before positioning for a further decline amid mixed fundamental cues.
The preliminary Corporate Goods Price Index (CGPI) published by the Bank of Japan (BoJ) showed that wholesale inflation increased by 0.7% in October, marking the first rise in three months. Moreover, the yearly rate accelerated to 7.1% from 6.8% in September, strengthening the case for an imminent BoJ rate hike in December. Adding to this, Japan's top currency diplomat Atsushi Mimura warned against excessive FX volatility, fueling intervention risks and providing a modest lift to the Japanese Yen (JPY).
The US Dollar (USD), on the other hand, consolidates a two-day rally to its highest level since April 2025 and exerts some downward pressure on the USD/JPY pair. However, the growing acceptance that the US Federal Reserve (Fed) will raise borrowing costs again and the possibility of a jumbo 50-basis-point (bps) rate hike in December continue to act as a tailwind for the USD. Moreover, the geopolitical risk premium remains in play amid the US-Iran standoff, which further supports the safe-haven Greenback.
President Donald Trump signaled that further US military action against Iran was unlikely for now, raising hopes that negotiations could bring an end to the conflict. That said, the US has repeatedly struck Iran’s Qeshm Island, while Tehran targeted an Omani island used to help ships navigate the Strait of Hormuz. This tempers expectations for a diplomatic resolution to the US-Iran conflict, which, along with hawkish Fed bets, favors USD bulls and backs the case for the emergence of dip-buying around the USD/JPY pair.
The USD/JPY pair maintains a bullish near-term bias above the 100-day Simple Moving Average (SMA) at 158.99. Spot prices consolidate just beneath the 61.8% Fibonacci retracement of the 152.88–164.00 rally at 159.75, which is followed by the 78.6% retracement at 161.62. On the downside, initial support emerges at the 100-day SMA at 158.99, ahead of the 50.0% retracement at 158.44. A deeper pullback would expose the 38.2% level at 157.13, with lower structural floors at 155.51 and 152.88.
(The technical analysis of this story was written with the help of an AI tool. Know more.)
The Bank of Japan (BoJ) is the Japanese central bank, which sets monetary policy in the country. Its mandate is to issue banknotes and carry out currency and monetary control to ensure price stability, which means an inflation target of around 2%.
The Bank of Japan embarked in an ultra-loose monetary policy in 2013 in order to stimulate the economy and fuel inflation amid a low-inflationary environment. The bank’s policy is based on Quantitative and Qualitative Easing (QQE), or printing notes to buy assets such as government or corporate bonds to provide liquidity. In 2016, the bank doubled down on its strategy and further loosened policy by first introducing negative interest rates and then directly controlling the yield of its 10-year government bonds. In March 2024, the BoJ lifted interest rates, effectively retreating from the ultra-loose monetary policy stance.
The Bank’s massive stimulus caused the Yen to depreciate against its main currency peers. This process exacerbated in 2022 and 2023 due to an increasing policy divergence between the Bank of Japan and other main central banks, which opted to increase interest rates sharply to fight decades-high levels of inflation. The BoJ’s policy led to a widening differential with other currencies, dragging down the value of the Yen. This trend partly reversed in 2024, when the BoJ decided to abandon its ultra-loose policy stance.
A weaker Yen and the spike in global energy prices led to an increase in Japanese inflation, which exceeded the BoJ’s 2% target. The prospect of rising salaries in the country – a key element fuelling inflation – also contributed to the move.
